docs.title: 7. Operational properties
docs.text:
• Stateless app, stateful disk: the container can be recreated freely. Only the data volume matters. Auto-restart + a persistent disk = self-healing after reboots.
  • Zero-dependency runtime: no DB, no cache, no message broker. Only the binary, a TLS proxy, and a disk.
  • Graceful shutdown (30s): lets in-flight writes finish and SSE goroutines exit cleanly before a container restart.
  • Teardown is one command (terraform destroy), so no stray paid resources linger.

docs.title: Network architecture
docs.text:
How traffic flows between browsers and the tournament app: HTTPS termination at a reverse proxy, plain HTTP to the app, real-time updates over Server-Sent Events (SSE), and the client-side resilience that keeps it working on flaky venue Wi-Fi.

Related: Software architecture · Infrastructure architecture

docs.title: 1. Edge topology
docs.text:
The app speaks plain HTTP. A TLS-terminating reverse proxy (Caddy, automatic Let's Encrypt) sits in front and streams SSE through unbuffered.

flowchart LR
    subgraph net["Venue / Internet"]
        op["Operator tablets"]
        vw["Viewer phones"]
    end

    subgraph host["Host (VM / container host)"]
        caddy["Caddy<br/>:80 redirect · :443 HTTPS<br/>auto TLS · streams SSE unbuffered"]
        app["bracket-creator mobile-app<br/>:8080 (HTTP, internal only)"]
        disk[("tournament-data/<br/>on persistent disk")]
    end

    op -->|HTTPS 443| caddy
    vw -->|HTTPS 443 + SSE| caddy
    caddy -->|HTTP reverse_proxy| app
    app --> disk
Port Where Purpose 443 Caddy (public) HTTPS for REST + SSE 80 Caddy (public) ACME challenge; redirect to 443 8080 app (internal) plain HTTP; never published directly (Caddy proxies it) 22 host (optional) SSH (restrict to your IP)

Proxy must stream, not buffer. SSE is a long-lived response. The Caddyfiles deliberately avoid flush_interval and response-buffering directives, because those would break the real-time event stream. (In production HTTPS comes from the proxy, so browser secure-context features work even though the app itself serves plain HTTP.)

docs.title: 2. Protocols on the wire
docs.text:
Two channels share the one HTTPS origin:

flowchart TB
    subgraph client["Browser SPA"]
        rest["REST calls<br/>fetch() JSON"]
        sse["1 long-lived SSE stream<br/>EventSource('/api/events')"]
    end
    subgraph server["mobile-app"]
        api["/api/* handlers<br/>(request/response)"]
        hub["SSE hub<br/>(fan-out)"]
    end
    rest -->|REST calls + auth header| api
    api -.->|after persist| hub
    hub ==>|SSE id + data frames| sse
  • REST: score, decision, and lineup writes, config, and participants. Every scoring tap (a point, a foul, an overtime period, an engi flag, a team bout's tie or fusensho, a fighter named for a bout, a representative pick, the representative bout's judges' decision) is an event sent to POST /api/competitions/{id}/matches/{mid}/score-events, in a batch of at most 64 from one device session. The server appends each event to the match's event log, replays the log in the order the taps were made, and answers 200 with one outcome per event, except a malformed batch (400). The answer also lists the gaps (the sequence numbers of that session's taps the server never received) and carries the match as stored, whose eventSeqs (per device session, the highest tap number the log holds) and turnedAway (each device tap the log holds that the server does not apply now, with its outcome) every later copy of the match carries too. Finishes, decisions, starts, reopens, sends back to the queue and corrections are whole writes, such as PUT /api/competitions/{id}/matches/{mid}/score; they also enter the match's log, and every device stamps them with the time they were made. Only the rule-bound writes (the taps, the whole writes of a match, lineups, team members, reinstatements and pool rank orders) go through the device's outbox (§4); setup edits, such as tournament and competition settings, the roster, check-in, the draw and announcements, are direct calls that are not kept for later. Auth is handled through the X-Tournament-Password header (two modes, §5; self-run mode allows unauthenticated scoring). Every response carries the X-App-Build header naming the git commit of the server build (or unknown), allowing clients to detect when a new server build is running.
  • SSE: one stream per client carrying match_updated, competition_started, competition_completed, competitor_status_updated, participants_updated, tournament_updated, schedule_updated, lineup_updated, draw_generated, draw_discarded, swiss_round_generated, announcement, password_reset and bracket_quarantined, plus the resilience control events resync_required and heartbeat. Every real event is stamped with a monotonic seq written as the SSE id: line, so the browser's Last-Event-ID advances automatically. A tap does not push by itself: the server replays the match and pushes the resulting match_updated. For a running match these pushes are held to at most four a second, with a final push carrying the newest state; any other push goes at once.

docs.title: 3. Real-time delivery & reconnect (SSE hub)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant B as Browser (EventSource)
    participant C as Caddy
    participant H as SSE hub

    B->>C: GET /api/events
    C->>H: proxied (unbuffered)
    H-->>B: id: N · data: event   (real-time, as matches change)
    Note over H: each event stamped seq=N,<br/>retained in a 200-event ring
    B--xH: Wi-Fi blip, connection drops
    B->>C: reconnect, new EventSource with ?lastEventId=N
    C->>H: proxied
    alt gap satisfiable from ring
        H-->>B: replay N+1 … head
    else ring rolled past N, or server restarted (seq reset)
        H-->>B: resync_required (full refetch)
    end
    H-->>B: heartbeat every 15s (observable frame)
  • Replay ring: DefaultHistorySize (200) recent events. The last id the client saw replays the gap. The client reconnects by opening a new EventSource, which sends no Last-Event-ID header, so it sends that id as the lastEventId query parameter (the header wins if both arrive).
  • resync_required: emitted when a gap-free replay is impossible (ring eviction or a server restart that reset seq). The client resets its lastSeq and full-refetches. Emitted without an id: line when head seq is 0 so it can't force Last-Event-ID to "0".
  • Observable heartbeat: a real {"type":"heartbeat","nowMs":<unix ms>} frame (no id:) every 15s, so the client can tell "quiet" from "dead". nowMs is the server clock at send time. It is a tripwire for a client whose own clock has drifted, not a source to set the clock from. A one-way push carries no round trip to correct against, so a delayed frame would drag the client's clock backwards. A client that sees a large divergence relearns the offset from the time endpoint instead.
  • Per-client buffered channel; a stalled client that can't drain is dropped (non-blocking send). Subscriber cap SSE_MAX_CLIENTS (default 5000).

docs.title: 4. Client resilience on flaky Wi-Fi
docs.text:
The client treats the link as unreliable by default. The following flows show how.

Two patterns carry scoring. On the server each match is event sourced: the match's score log holds the taps and the whole writes made to it, and the match shown to everyone is rebuilt by replaying that log in the order the changes were made. On the device a transactional outbox holds every tap and every write: it is stored in the browser before anything is sent, so a score is never only in the memory of a page. The outbox sends a match's entries in the order they were made, until the server confirms each, and the confirmation is idempotent, because a tap carries its own id and a repeated id is recognised and logged once.

There is deliberately no message broker between them. The queue that matters is on the tablet, because the tablet is the part that goes offline; a broker in the venue or the cloud would hold nothing the tablet does not already hold. The order that matters is when each tap was made, which the replay restores from the tap's own stamp, so a queue that preserved arrival order would add nothing. And the app is one binary that keeps its data in files, so a broker would be a second system to install, secure and keep running at a tournament for no gain.

Only a confirmed write ever empties the queue. A write that cannot be confirmed is never dropped in silence: it is either kept and retried, parked until the operator can fix the cause, or, when the server refuses it outright, removed with a visible notice naming the reason, or discarded by the operator from the match's score editor after a confirm, when the server keeps refusing it. A write is never removed for its age: however long it waited, it is sent, and the server orders it by when it was made. Entries of one match are sent strictly in the order they were made, so one that does not land holds back that match's later entries and no other match's.

The cycle for one match's taps:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant Op as Operator
    participant Ob as Outbox (localStorage, shared by tabs)
    participant S as Server (score-events)
    participant Log as Match event log
    participant St as Landed and told tap records (browser storage)

    Op->>Ob: tap (id, device session, seq, stamp)
    Ob-->>Op: answered pending at once, the board shows it
    Note over Ob: per match, strictly in the order made,<br/>consecutive taps batched (up to 64)
    Ob->>S: POST score-events (batch)
    alt offline, or 5xx / 429 / 403
        S--xOb: no answer, or an error
        Note over Ob: kept, sent again later (safe: same ids)
    else 200
        S->>Log: append each new tap, replay by stamp
        S-->>Ob: one outcome per tap + gaps + the match as stored
        Note over Ob: applied / recorded / duplicate: leaves quietly<br/>clock_skew: re-stamped once, sent again<br/>any other outcome (matchClosed, noTarget, ...):<br/>leaves, the operator is told
        Ob->>St: note the taps that landed
        opt gaps name seqs the server never got
            Ob->>S: those taps sent again at once
        end
    end
    S-->>Ob: a later copy of the match (a push or a fetch) lists turnedAway
    St-->>Op: a landed tap it lists is told once per device
flowchart TD
    submit["Operator taps a point, or submits a Finish / decision / lineup"] --> q["Stored in the outbox first<br/>(localStorage, one entry per tap or write)<br/>the board shows it at once"]
    q --> flush["Background flush, per match in the order made<br/>taps in batches of up to 64<br/>(12s timeout, backoff to 8s max)"]
    flush -->|2xx whole write| done["Confirmed<br/>queue entry cleared<br/>(a held write is answered with a notice)"]
    flush -->|2xx per-tap answers| ans["Each tap answered one by one"]
    ans -->|applied / recorded / duplicate| tapdone["Leaves the queue quietly<br/>(the same id twice is logged once)"]
    ans -->|clock_skew| restamp["Re-stamped once, same id, sent again"]
    restamp --> flush
    ans -->|any other outcome<br/>such as matchClosed or noTarget| told["Leaves the queue, the operator is told<br/>(in the editor + one alert per pass)"]
    ans -->|gaps: seqs the server never got| resend["Those taps are sent again"]
    resend --> flush
    flush -->|offline| q
    flush -->|5xx / 429 / 403<br/>server error or misconfigured| retrying["Stays queued, keeps retrying, holds back only that match's later entries<br/>10 rejections: notice + 'Not saving' in the header count<br/>+ 'Discard held result' in its editor"]
    retrying --> flush
    retrying -->|operator confirms Discard held result| discarded["Discarded: that write only"]
    flush -->|401<br/>invalid password| parked["Parked: stops retrying<br/>header count + editor notice show 'Sign in to save'"]
    parked -->|operator signs in| flush
    flush -->|other 4xx on a batch of taps<br/>such as a 400| parkedtaps["Parked, never dropped<br/>holds back that match's later entries<br/>until the operator discards it"]
    flush -->|other 4xx on a whole write: 400 / 413 / 409| refused["Discarded, permanently refused<br/>notice names the match + reason"]
    online["browser 'online' event, tab visible again"] --> flush

Not every write is an outbox entry. The rule-bound writes, the ones the server orders and judges against what the match or the team already holds, are; setup edits are direct calls:

flowchart LR
    rule["Rule-bound writes<br/>taps · score writes (start, record bout, finish, correction)<br/>decisions · reopen · send back to the queue · queue it and reopen<br/>court move · time change<br/>representative bout added or removed · kachinuki bout removed<br/>match lineup saved or removed · starting lineup saved<br/>team member added or renamed · reinstatement · pool rank order (chusen)"]
    rule --> ob["Outbox<br/>(localStorage, shared by tabs)<br/>answered pending at once"]
    ob --> order["Sent per match (or per team, competitor<br/>or competition) strictly in the order made"]
    order --> srv["Server"]
    setup["Setup edits<br/>tournament and competition settings<br/>roster, seeds, check-in<br/>draw, competition start and completion<br/>Swiss rounds · league tie-breaks<br/>announcements · sponsors · branding · import"]
    setup --> direct["Direct REST call<br/>sent at once, not kept for later<br/>an error goes back to the page at once"]
    direct --> srv

The Participants page saves the whole competitor list in one call (a typed seed, a row moved, a shuffle, seeds cleared or read from a file, a pasted list applied), while registration desks check competitors in and add them at the same time. Two rules keep each desk's change:

  • A list save never writes a check-in. Every competitor keeps the check-in the server holds for them, whatever the list says. Only the check-in calls check a competitor in or out.
  • A list save names the list it was built from (rosterVersion, which every competition answer carrying the list includes). When another desk has added, removed, renamed, moved or seeded a competitor since, the server refuses the save with 409 roster_changed, writes nothing, and answers with the list as it stands. The page shows that list at once, applies the operator's change to it again (the seed, the move, the shuffle) and sends it straight away, so both desks' changes land. A pasted list is the one exception: it would replace a list the operator never saw, so the page saves nothing, says the list changed on another device and keeps the pasted list in the box for one tap to apply it again. A check-in does not count as a change of the list.
flowchart LR
    subgraph watchdog["SSE liveness"]
        arm["watchdog armed on connect"] --> silent{"no message/heartbeat for 35s?"}
        silent -->|yes| reconnect["close + reconnect<br/>(backoff + jitter)"]
        silent -->|no| arm
    end
    vis["visibilitychange: tab → visible"] --> rc["reconnectEvents() + refetch"]
    back["browser 'online' event"] --> rco["reconnectEvents()"]
    rco --> reopen["stream reopens after a loss"]
    reconnect --> reopen
    reopen --> rf["refetch (jittered)"]

Key client mechanisms (all in web-mobile/js/api_client.jsx + consumers):

Concern Mechanism Half-open / stalled sockets 12s write timeouts, 35s SSE silence watchdog (armed at connect, not only onopen) Reconnect storms exponential backoff + jitter (vs. a fixed delay) Lost writes durable outbox persisted to localStorage, retried until it lands, with no age limit; survives tab refresh. Every tap and every rule-bound write (setup edits are direct calls) is stored in the outbox in the moment it is made, before anything is sent, so the browser never holds a score only in memory. Each entry belongs to a match, or to a team (a starting lineup, a team member added, renamed or cleared), a competitor (a reinstatement) or a competition (a pool rank order), and a flush pass sends the entries of each strictly in the order they were made (their stamp, then the order they were stored). One that does not land (offline, a 5xx that keeps coming back, a sign-in it waits for, or an entry it must follow) ends its turn for the pass and holds back the later entries of the same match, team, competitor or competition, so a write made after another on the same device never reaches the server first. The others go on. Consecutive taps of one device session go as one batch of at most 64. A tap is idempotent by its event id: sent twice, it is logged once and answered as a duplicate, so a lost answer is harmless. A court move, a time change, a lineup save, a match lineup's removal, a reinstatement, a pool rank order and a team member's rename or cleared name are taken in the order they arrive, so each carries a write id, and the server answers a late duplicate as recorded without applying it again. A team member's add carries the id the device made for the member, so the same add sent again is answered with the member as stored. A reopen, a send back to the queue, a queue-it-and-reopen, a kachinuki bout's removal and a representative bout's add or removal each carry a write id too, which the match's score log keeps, so a late duplicate of any of them is also answered as recorded. A lineup save's positions are still ordered by when each was changed (changedAt), and a match lineup's removal by when it was made (removedAt), so a late copy of an earlier save never puts an older value back. A later running update never takes the place of a queued Finish or decision, and a decision and a score for the same match are both kept; a tap never folds into anything. Only a score write folds into the score write queued just before it, when that one has not been sent (a running update into a running update, a Finish into either, as when the editor re-sends a held Finish), naming every group either changed. A lineup save is the other write that folds: it joins a queued save of the same lineup, which then names every position either changed, with the later value where both changed one. A refusal on replay is always reported, never taken as success. Every tab of the app shares the stored outbox. A tab saving its queue merges into it: it adds its own writes, keeps the newer copy where two tabs hold the same entry, and removes only the writes it settled. Each tab also takes up the writes another tab stores, so a write queued in a tab that then closes is still sent by a tab left open. A write two tabs hold can be sent by both, which is harmless, because the server orders writes by their stamps and recognises a repeated id (refer to Order of writes in this table) Order of writes nothing a device sends is thrown away, and changes are put in the order they were made (the write's or the tap's own stamp), never the order they arrive. A device stamps a write with its estimate of the server's time, and never earlier than the match it was made against: two devices' estimates can differ by up to the 5 s the server accepts, so a change made a moment after a write stamped by a device running ahead would otherwise read as older than the write it changed. A tap is stamped with the same rule, against the match as it was when the operator tapped, so a change another device makes afterwards never moves it. The stamp is therefore the later of the device's time and the stamp of the match as the operator saw it plus 1 ms, never more than 4 s past the device's time. Taps are replayed by their stamps on the server, and a whole write names the groups of the match it changes (changed: points, result, encho, flags, rep, each side's representative pick, repPickA and repPickB, or one bout row, bout:<position>). The score editor works this out by comparing what it sends with the match it was showing. The server applies each named group only if the write is not older than the last change applied to that group, and never touches a group the write does not name, so two devices changing different things both land whatever order they arrive in. A named group a newer change outranks is not applied: its value is kept in the match's history (GET /api/competitions/:id/matches/:mid/history), which the score editors show under History. A write applied in part answers with heldGroups; one none of which applied answers {"applied": false, "reason": "superseded"} with the same list, and the editor says "Not applied" rather than "Not saved". Once a finish or a decision is recorded, a tap or a scoring write made after it is not applied either: the finish stands, the change is kept in the history, and the answer adds heldReason: "match_closed" (a tap's outcome is matchClosed), on which the editor tells the operator that the match is finished and to tap Correct. Arrival order does not change the outcome. A tap that reached the server before a finish made earlier is applied at first; when the finish arrives, the tap is moved to the history (an entry of its own, at its own time) and the finish is answered applied, naming it in displacedGroups with heldReason: "match_closed" and no heldGroups; the editor says "Saved" and what was moved, and a held finish replayed this way raises one information alert. The first recorded result stands: a later finish or decision from a device that did not see the result in force is held in the same way, whichever arrived first, and so is one that would replace a knockout result after the next match was played or started (heldReason downstream_knockout_played or downstream_knockout_running). A representative pick made after its representative bout was removed is moved to the history the same way when the removal arrives, and that answer names it in displacedGroups with no heldReason. Where the outbox folds a queued running update into a later one, the later one names every group either changed. The same holds for the writes that are not score sheets: an older save the same device had already followed with a newer one (an out-of-order delivery after a reconnect) is kept whole in the history as an "older revision of this board"; an engi result is ordered by when it was saved, its flags and the winner they decide kept together. A queued decision or finish whose first send landed but whose answer was lost is answered as recorded when it is sent again: the same write under the same stamp changes nothing, so it is not asked for a correction reason and nothing is written to the match; the match's history gains a line saying the write arrived and changed nothing Edits not yet sent a score editor holds nothing back on a running match. Every tap (a point, a foul, an overtime period, a flag, a bout's tie or fusensho, a fighter named for a bout, a representative pick, the representative bout's judges' decision) goes into the outbox the moment it is made, in the order it was made, and the board shows it at once, as the server's match with the device's pending taps on top. There is no autosave and no save delay, and nothing to lose by closing the editor, moving to another match, hiding the tab or reloading the page. A tap carries the time it was made, not the time it is sent, so it never outranks a result another device recorded after it. The exceptions are a few entries that are not taps: on a running match a Mark draw, a hantei pick and a removed withdrawal are held in the editor until Finish (or until a decision carries them). On a match that is not running (queued, or finished and being corrected) the editor holds everything the operator enters as a draft, sent by Start, Finish or Save correction. Leaving with entries not yet sent, by closing the editor, moving to another match or leaving the page, asks first with one warning, "Your unsaved entries will be discarded. anyway?", with Discard entries and Keep entries, and nothing is sent until the operator answers Taps the server does not apply a tap is answered one by one. An applied, already recorded or repeated tap leaves the queue quietly. A tap refused for a clock too far ahead is stamped again once and sent under the same id. Any other tap the server answered without applying (the match is finished, matchClosed; the mark it names is not there, noTarget; made before a result that never saw it, beforeBaseline; a self-run limit) leaves the queue and is told to the operator in the editor and in one alert per pass. The answer also lists the gaps, the taps of the device's session the server never received, and the outbox sends the ones it still holds again at once. Every copy of the match names, per device session, the highest tap number its log holds (eventSeqs), so a screen never counts a pending tap twice, and lists the device taps the server does not apply now (turnedAway): a tap first answered as applied can be turned away later, when a finish that never saw it arrives after it, and the device that made it tells its operator once, from the newest copy of the match it has seen, in one tab. Two tabs reading the same tap at the same moment can each tell it, so the notice may come twice, but it is never lost. A tap sent while the match is neither running nor finished is not logged and is told the same way. A tap on a finished match is logged and answered matchClosed. A whole batch the server refuses with a 4xx other than 401 is parked instead of dropped Server errors (5xx / 429), and 403 write stays queued and keeps retrying until it lands, holding back only that match's later entries; after 10 consecutive rejections the operator gets a notice and the header count reads "Not saving", and the match's score editor offers Discard held result, which discards that write and nothing else after a confirm. The held-writes count in the admin topbar opens a list of every held write (score updates, results, decisions, lineups), where any write that keeps failing can be discarded the same way, one at a time; a write only waiting for the connection cannot be discarded there. The public page shows the same held-writes count in its bottom-left corner (only while a write is held) and opens the same list. On this server 403 is never a bad credential (that is 401): it means the tournament is not configured yet, or is missing its password. Only an admin fixing the server state clears it, so signing in again cannot help and the write keeps retrying instead of parking Invalid credential (401) the one 4xx a retry can fix: the write is parked, not discarded, stops retrying, and shows "Sign in to save"; signing in again re-sends it with the new credential, together with every other queued write still carrying the refused password (one queued after it, before its own 401 came back), so one sign-in is enough. A write queued without a password (a competitor's in a self-run event) is never given one Other non-retryable 4xx (400 validation, 413, generic 409) a whole write is discarded (it can never succeed on retry), and the operator always gets a visible notice naming the match and the server's reason. A batch of taps the server refuses with a 4xx other than 401 (a 400, say) is not discarded: it is parked, stays out of the board and the display, and holds back that match's later entries until the operator discards it from the editor or the held-writes list, with one alert Missed events replay from the last event id the client saw (?lastEventId=), checkSeqGap on every event → scoped refetch; resync_required. A stream that reopens after it was lost also refetches everything, jittered over 2s so a venue's devices do not all ask at once: replay does not resend an event the page received whose refetch then failed because the device could not fetch Back online the browser's online event forces a reconnect, and the reopened stream refetches as above (the stream can outlive the outage, so it is not left to report a loss itself) Tab resume visibilitychange → force reconnect + refetch False success terminal writes show pending / parked / still-retrying / failure state, never a false "saved"; a write dropped because the stored entry was corrupt also raises a visible notice at page load, never a silent loss. The admin topbar counts this tab's held writes after the connection status ("Offline: 1 result not sent", "Sending 1 result…", "Not saving: 1 result"), and the public page shows the count in its bottom-left corner while a write is held, so a held result stays visible after the editor that held it closes, and the connection status reads "Reconnecting…" while held writes fail for network reasons. When held finished results land, one success toast per flush says so ("1 finished result sent."). Every write passes through the outbox, so a result that lands at once raises none of these (the success toast appears only for results that had been held) Storage full if the browser can't persist the queue (storage quota exhausted), that is surfaced to the operator rather than swallowed: an alert, and the queued write answers persisted: false, so its score editor says "Not sent yet: keep this page open until the connection returns." instead of "saved on this device" Credential change queue cleared on logout (the operator is asked to confirm first if writes are still unsent). On password_reset the queued writes are parked instead: the old password is removed from every stored write, every tab's included, and they are re-sent once the operator signs in again (no stale-password retries)

docs.text:
flowchart TD
    req["Request with X-Tournament-Password"] --> verifier{"PasswordVerifier<br/>(auth_source.go)"}

docs.title: 7. Scale limit = egress
docs.text: Because every real-time update is fanned out to every connected viewer, network egress is the practical ceiling, not CPU/RAM. Refer to Infrastructure architecture for per-tier audience guidance (for example, GCP free tier compared with Oracle for large events).

docs.title: 5. Write path: recording a score (ACID + broadcast)
docs.text:
A scoring tap and a finishing write take different doors into the same engine. A tap is an event: the browser stores it in its outbox at once, and the outbox sends it to the match's score events endpoint. The engine appends it to the match's event log, replays the log in the order the taps were made, writes the match the replay produces, and keeps a history line, all in one transaction.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant SPA as Browser SPA (outbox)
    participant MW as auth middleware
    participant H as handlers_score_events.go
    participant E as engine
    participant S as state.Store (WAL)
    participant HUB as SSE hub
    participant OTHERS as other clients

    SPA->>SPA: tap stored in the outbox, board updated at once
    SPA->>MW: POST /api/competitions/:id/matches/:mid/score-events (batch of taps)
    MW->>MW: verify X-Tournament-Password
    MW->>H: authorized
    H->>E: RecordScoreEventsTx(...)
    E->>S: WithTransaction → append events/{matchId}.jsonl, stage the replayed match + history
    S->>S: WAL commit → atomic write (fsync + rename) → done
    S-->>E: persisted
    E-->>H: one outcome per tap + gaps + the match as stored (carries eventSeqs, turnedAway)
    H->>HUB: Broadcast(match_updated)  [after persist, a running match at most 4 a second]
    HUB-->>OTHERS: SSE event (id: seq)
    H-->>SPA: 200 (outbox clears applied, recorded and duplicate taps<br/>clock_skew ones re-stamped and sent again, gaps sent again<br/>turnedAway told once per device)

A finish, a correction and the other whole writes use their own routes, such as the one below (a decision and a reopen have theirs, POST /decision and POST /reopen). They are outbox entries too, and they enter the same event log as a baseline, so a tap and a whole write are ordered against each other by the time each was made.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant SPA as Browser SPA (outbox)
    participant MW as auth middleware
    participant H as handlers_match.go
    participant E as engine
    participant S as state.Store (WAL)
    participant HUB as SSE hub
    participant OTHERS as other clients

    SPA->>SPA: write stored in the outbox, answered pending at once,<br/>sent after the match's earlier entries
    SPA->>MW: PUT /api/competitions/:id/matches/:mid/score
    MW->>MW: verify X-Tournament-Password
    MW->>H: authorized
    H->>E: RecordMatchResultWithIneligibilityTx(...)
    E->>S: WithTransaction → stage writes (intents)
    S->>S: WAL commit → atomic write (fsync + rename) → done
    S-->>E: persisted
    E-->>H: result (+ eligibility status)
    H->>HUB: Broadcast(match_updated, ...)  [after persist]
    HUB-->>OTHERS: SSE event (id: seq)
    H-->>SPA: 200 result

Core invariant: persist then broadcast. A write is durable (fsync + atomic rename, WAL for multi-file changes) before the 200 and before any SSE fan-out. Scoring is ACID. A legitimate operator change is never dropped.

docs.title: Key design rules
docs.text:
Refer to DESIGN.md for the full visual design system.

  • Persist before broadcast; scoring is ACID; never drop a legitimate operator change.
  • Use layout/sheet constants (internal/helper/constants.go), never string literals.
  • errcheck is enforced in production code: propagate or log, never _ =.
  • Aka (Red) / Shiro (White) are positional, distinguished by treatment, not hue alone.

docs.title: Set up your machine
docs.text:
bracket-creator is written in Go.

Prerequisites:

  • Go 1.27.3+

Other things you might need to run the tests:

  • Docker

Clone bracket-creator anywhere:

git clone git@github.com:gitrgoliveira/bracket-creator.git

cd into the directory and install the dependencies:

make local/deps

docs.title: Test your change
docs.text:
You can create a branch for your changes and try to build from the source as you go:

make go/build

When you are satisfied with the changes, run:

make go/test
make go/test-race

Before you commit the changes, run:

make pre-commit

docs.title: Test the bracket generator web UI
docs.text:
make run          # starts on localhost:8080
PORT=8081 make run

Open the browser and walk through bracket generation manually. Type checking and unit tests do not exercise the UI rendering path.

docs.title: Test the mobile / tournament app
docs.text:
make run-mobile                                     # localhost:8080, data dir ./tournament-data
PORT=8082 make run-mobile                           # custom port
TOURNAMENT_DATA_DIR=/path/to/data make run-mobile  # custom data dir

The binary reads PORT, BIND_ADDRESS, and TOURNAMENT_DATA_DIR directly, so they also work without make:

TOURNAMENT_DATA_DIR=/path PORT=8082 ./bin/bracket-creator mobile-app

An explicit --folder, --port, or --bind flag still overrides the env var.

Important: web-mobile/ is a Preact/JSX frontend compiled by esbuild into web-mobile/dist/ and then embedded into the Go binary at build time. Any change to the web-mobile/js/ sources (.js or .jsx) or web-mobile/css/*.css requires the following:

  1. Rebuild the JS bundle: cd web-mobile && npm run build (or npx esbuild ...; refer to the project Makefile)
  2. Rebuild the binary: make go/build
  3. Restart the server: make run-mobile

Editing these frontend sources and refreshing the browser does not pick up changes. The browser still gets the embedded bundle from the last binary build.

docs.title: Run the end-to-end journeys
docs.text:
The end-to-end journeys drive the tournament app in a real browser, the way a court operator and a spectator use it: an iPad-sized touch screen for the operator and a phone for the public pages. Run them before you open a pull request that changes web-mobile/; the pull request template asks for it.

make e2e                                              # every journey
make e2e E2E_ARGS='journeys/smoke.spec.mjs'           # one journey file
make e2e E2E_ARGS='--grep "score on a shiaijo"'       # one test by title
make e2e E2E_ARGS='journeys/smoke.spec.mjs --headed'  # watch it run

make e2e builds the binary, then runs each journey file against its own server on a free port with an empty data folder. You need Go, node with npm, and a network connection: the first run installs the harness's packages and its Chromium, and every build downloads the frontend libraries. The journeys are not part of make go/test and do not run in CI.

The harness's own guide, scripts/e2e/README.md, covers the rest: the devices, the console policy that fails a journey on a browser error, where screenshots and traces are written, how to add a journey, and what to do when a journey finds a bug.

docs.title: Regenerate the documentation screenshots
docs.text:
Every screenshot and video under docs/screenshots/ and docs/videos/ is captured from the running application by a script, so a picture cannot quietly drift from the product it shows. If your change alters anything a user sees, recapture what it reaches with make docs/media SINCE=main before you open the pull request.

make docs/screenshots                        # the application screenshots
make docs/videos                             # the application videos
make docs/media                              # both

make docs/screenshots NAME=mobile-dashboard  # one capture
make docs/screenshots FAMILY=editors         # one group
make docs/screenshots SINCE=main             # only the groups your changes reach

You need node and python3; the first run installs the rest. A run writes to scripts/screenshots/out/, never into docs/ directly, and ends by listing only the screenshots that differ from the committed ones. Look at those and copy across the ones whose change you meant to make. Anything reported as unchanged needs no review. Videos are never compared, so copy a video only when your change alters what it shows.

The harness's own guide, scripts/screenshots/README.md, covers the rest: how SINCE= decides what to capture, what a changed line tells you, what to do when a capture you did not touch appears in the list, how a capture must be seeded, and how to add one.

docs.title: create-knockout
docs.text:
Generates a Knockout Only bracket: a direct single-elimination tree with no pool phase.

bracket-creator create-knockout [flags]

Note

create-playoffs is kept as an alias and still works, so existing scripts that invoke it do not need to change.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Simple two-court bracket:

bracket-creator create-knockout -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx

Single court, seeded:

bracket-creator create-knockout \
  -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx \
  -c 1 --seeds seeds.csv

Team tournament across two courts with zekken names:

bracket-creator create-knockout \
  -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx \
  -t 3 -c 2 -z

docs.title: Shiai-jo count
docs.text:
--courts takes 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. The tree is split into one block per shiai-jo. Those blocks merge in pairs, so the count has to halve cleanly all the way down. Any other value stops the command with an error naming the counts to use instead, and the error always offers 1.

Being even is not enough on its own. With -c 6 the six blocks pair off into three, but three cannot pair off again. One of them would then reach the final having fought a round fewer than the other two. -c 6 and -c 10 are therefore refused, just as -c 3, -c 5 and -c 7 are.

A single shiai-jo is always allowed: -c 1 prints the whole bracket as one shiai-jo's pages. A knockout bracket has no pool finishers to cross between shiai-jo. It is seeded first, then cut into shiai-jo blocks, so the partner-shiai-jo crossing described for create-pools does not apply here. 16 is the highest. It is also the most shiai-jo a tournament can have, so 32 is out of reach.

This is a per-tournament-file rule, not a rule about your venue. A hall with three shiai-jo generates one file for two shiai-jo and another for one, and runs both at the same time. Refer to create-pools for the same rule on the pools command, and How many shiai-jo a competition can use for the full explanation.

docs.title: Seeding
docs.text:
Works the same as create-pools; top seeds are placed on opposite sides of the bracket so they can only meet in the final. Refer to the input format for the seeds CSV layout.

Competitor numbers follow that seeded bracket order, not the order participants were listed in the input file. The top seed is numbered first, and every other competitor's number follows their position in the bracket, top to bottom. The Data and Names to Print sheets list competitors in that same order.

docs.text: Sheet Contents Data Raw participant list Time Estimator Expected duration per phase Elimination Matches Match schedule Names to Print A3-ready name labels Tree (one per court) Visual bracket tree

docs.text:

bracket-creator create-pools [flags]

Mutually exclusive with --players. --pool-winners -w 2 Players that qualify from each pool; refer to Qualifiers per pool --extra-qualifiers (none) "" Send extra qualifiers from oversized pools, or fit pool sizes exactly to the bracket; refer to Extra qualifiers --round-robin -r false Force full round-robin in every pool --team-matches -t 0 Players per team (0 = individual tournament) --with-zekken-name -z false Use second CSV column as zekken display name --seeds (none) (none) CSV file with seed rankings --determined -d false Do not shuffle input order --single-tree (none) false Produce one tree sheet instead of one per court --number-prefix -n (none) Letter prefix for competitor numbers (for example, K produces K1, K2, …). docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Minimal: two courts, random draw:

bracket-creator create-pools -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx

Four courts, pools of up to 5, top 2 qualify, full round-robin:

bracket-creator create-pools \
  -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx \
  -c 4 -m 5 -w 2 -r

Team tournament (3 players per team, 2 courts):

bracket-creator create-pools \
  -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx \
  -t 3 -c 2

With zekken names and seeding:

bracket-creator create-pools \
  -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx \
  -z --seeds seeds.csv

docs.title: Shiai-jo count
docs.text:
--courts takes 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16. The elimination tree gives each shiai-jo its own block of the bracket. The blocks then merge in pairs, so the count has to halve cleanly all the way down. Any other value stops the command with an error naming the counts to use instead, and the error always offers 1.

Being even is not enough on its own. With -c 6 the six blocks pair off into three, but three cannot pair off again. One of them would then reach the final having fought a round fewer than the other two. -c 6 and -c 10 are therefore refused, just as -c 3, -c 5 and -c 7 are.

A single shiai-jo is always allowed. With two or more qualifiers per pool (-w 2 and above), -c 1 splits its block into two halves that act as partner shiai-jo, producing the same bracket shape as a -c 2 run. With -w 1, nothing crosses between shiai-jo: the block stays whole, and each bye is chosen from every pool winner on it. 16 is the highest. It is also the most shiai-jo a tournament can have, so 32 is out of reach.

The draw also never uses more shiai-jo than there are pools, because a shiai-jo with no pools of its own would own an empty block. When you ask for more, the count steps down to the largest allowed value that fits. The file is generated without an error: with 7 pools, -c 8 produces a draw on 4 shiai-jo.

This is a per-tournament-file rule, not a rule about your venue. A hall with three shiai-jo generates one file for two shiai-jo and another for one, and runs both at the same time. Refer to How many shiai-jo a competition can use for the full explanation.

docs.title: Qualifiers per pool
docs.text:
--pool-winners sets how many players advance from each pool into the elimination tree. It also changes the shape of the draw, because each shiai-jo gets its own block of the bracket and shiai-jo are paired up into opposite halves:

-w What happens in the draw 1 Nothing crosses. Every qualifier is its own shiai-jo's pool winner and stays in that shiai-jo's block, so first-round matches are between pools of the same shiai-jo. 2 Pool winners stay in their own shiai-jo's block; runners-up cross to the partner shiai-jo's block. Partners are in opposite halves, so a pool's two qualifiers can only meet in the final. 3 As for 2, plus the third qualifier crosses to the other pair of shiai-jo, in the half that does not hold the pool winner. All three land in different quarters of the draw.

Higher values continue the same rotation, but a bracket has only four quarters. From the fifth qualifier per pool onward, two of a pool's qualifiers must share one.

Byes follow from the size of each block, not the total field. A block with an even number of competitors gets none. A block with an odd number gets exactly one, awarded first to a seeded pool's winner. Refer to The knockout draw for the full rules and worked examples.

docs.title: Extra qualifiers
docs.text:
--extra-qualifiers changes how many finishers each pool sends up, instead of every pool sending the same number:

Value Behaviour "" (default) Standard: every pool sends --pool-winners qualifiers; unfilled bracket slots become byes. larger-pools A pool larger than the minimum pool size sends one extra qualifier, crossed to a neighbouring shiai-jo, on top of the usual number. It always fights in the first round and never byes. fill-bracket Pools are cut so that pool winners, plus a handful of drafted second places, exactly fill the bracket with no byes. The drafts come from seeded pools in seed order (--seeds), with pools larger than the minimum as the fallback when there are not enough seeds.

Both larger-pools and fill-bracket require -p (minimum pool size, not -m) and -w 1; the command refuses any other combination. Refer to How many qualify from each pool for the full explanation and worked examples, including when each mode can and cannot build a draw for a given entrant count and shiai-jo count.

Minimum pool size 3, one qualifier per pool, with the Oversized send +1 behaviour:

bracket-creator create-pools \
  -f participants.csv -o tournament.xlsx \
  -p 3 -w 1 -c 4 --extra-qualifiers larger-pools

docs.title: Seeding
docs.text:
Seeding distributes top competitors so they land in separate pools and on opposite sides of each court's elimination bracket.

Create a seeds CSV:

Rank,Name
1,Cersei Lannister
2,Daenerys Targaryen
3,Eddard Stark

Pass it with --seeds seeds.csv. Names must match the participant name exactly, including accents. Both lists are title-cased on read, so only differences beyond each word's first letter matter. Unseeded participants are placed randomly around the seeds.

The rank order matters in the elimination tree as well as in the pool draw. Seeds 1 and 3 land in one half, and seeds 2 and 4 in the other, each in its own quarter. Refer to Seeding in the knockout draw.

docs.title: Output sheets
docs.text:
The generated Excel file contains:

Sheet Contents Data Raw participant list Time Estimator Expected duration per phase Pool Draw Pool assignments grouped by court Pool Matches Individual match schedule Elimination Matches Knockout bracket match schedule Names to Print A3-ready name labels Tree (one per court) Visual bracket tree for display

docs.title: hash-password
docs.text:
Produces a bcrypt hash for use with the mobile-app command's locked mode. Operators set the resulting hash in the TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH environment variable so the running server can compare incoming X-Tournament-Password headers against it without storing the plaintext.

bracket-creator hash-password [plaintext]

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The command reads the plaintext from one of two sources, in this order:

  1. Positional argument: bracket-creator hash-password mysecret. Convenient for ad-hoc use, but the password is recorded in shell history. Suitable for development.
  2. Standard input (when no argument is supplied): read one line of stdin. The terminal echoes what the operator types. The command does not disable echo or print a prompt. For production rotation, pipe from a secrets manager or here-doc rather than typing the password interactively. Recommended path because it avoids shell-history leakage.

Bcrypt has a hard 72-byte limit on the input. Passwords longer than that are rejected up-front rather than silently truncated.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Single line on stdout: the bcrypt hash (for example, $2a$10$tq9jkGYsf1ttx0ZM.UUrxezVBcO4aZaS.dVRY73xC5lwEvTJLcMc6). Cost is bcrypt.DefaultCost (10), fine for admin-facing endpoints (~50-100 ms per verify) and not worth tuning until a real load problem appears.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Pass the password as an argument:

bracket-creator hash-password mysecret

Pipe it from another command:

echo -n "$MY_SECRET" | bracket-creator hash-password

Capture the hash into a shell variable and start the tournament app in locked mode:

HASH=$(printf '%s' "$MY_SECRET" | bracket-creator hash-password)
TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH="$HASH" \
  bracket-creator mobile-app --lock-password -f ./tournament-data

Refer to the mobile-app command reference for how the hash is consumed at startup.

docs.title: mobile-app
docs.text:
Starts the tournament management server (Preact UI + REST/SSE backend). Used on the day of the tournament for drawing pools, recording scores, and pushing real-time updates to spectator screens.

bracket-creator mobile-app [flags]

Refer to the Tournament app guide for a full walkthrough of the UI.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: Flag Short Default Description --folder -f . Folder containing tournament.md and competitions/. Created at startup if it does not exist. --port -p 8080 (or $PORT) Port to listen on --bind -b localhost (or $BIND_ADDRESS) Address to bind to. Use 0.0.0.0 to reach the server from other devices on the LAN. --lock-password (none) unset (or $LOCK_PASSWORD=true) Switch to locked mode. Requires TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH. Refer to Authentication.

docs.text: Variable Used by Description PORT --port default Initial value for --port if the flag isn't set. BIND_ADDRESS --bind default Initial value for --bind if the flag isn't set. LOCK_PASSWORD --lock-password default true enables locked mode without passing the flag. TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH locked mode auth Bcrypt hash of the admin password. Required when --lock-password is set. Generate with hash-password. TOURNAMENT_ADMIN_PASSWORD_HASH nothing Ignored. When it is set, the server logs a line at startup saying so. The admin password above covers every action. Refer to Upgrading from an earlier release.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The server has two authentication modes for the admin console; viewer routes are always public.

docs.title: File mode (default)
docs.text:
The admin password is stored plaintext in tournament-data/tournament.md and compared by exact-string match. Set the password during the in-app Create tournament flow, or edit tournament.md directly.

  • POST /api/tournament/reset needs no password but answers only a request from the machine running the server (a loopback address) that is addressed to a loopback name: localhost, 127.0.0.1 or [::1]. Any other request, from another machine or addressed by another name, gets 403 with the code reset_local_only. If you've forgotten the current password, browse to http://localhost:<port>/reset on the machine running the server to set a new one. In a Docker container run with -p, a browser on the host reaches the server through the container network, not loopback, so the reset is refused there too; edit tournament.md in the mounted data folder instead.
  • GET /api/auth-config returns {"mode": "file", "resetEnabled": true}.

docs.title: Locked mode (--lock-password)
docs.text:
The on-disk password is ignored. Authentication compares the X-Tournament-Password header against a bcrypt hash from the TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH environment variable.

Generate the hash, piping the secret in rather than typing it (refer to hash-password for the input rules):

printf '%s' "$MY_ADMIN_SECRET" | bracket-creator hash-password

Start the server with the hash:

TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH='$2a$10$...' \
  bracket-creator mobile-app --lock-password -f ./tournament-data
  • POST /api/tournament/reset returns 404. The /reset SPA route still serves the embedded page, but renders an "operator-disabled" message instead of the form. The AuthModal also hides the "Forgot password?" link.
  • GET /api/auth-config returns {"mode": "locked", "resetEnabled": false}.
  • The server refuses to start if the env var is empty or malformed (fail-closed; no silent fallback to file mode).
  • Rotation requires restarting with a new hash. The hash is read once at startup.

Recommended for any deployment reachable over the internet. The plaintext-in-file pattern of file mode is intended for trusted-network use only.

docs.title: Operational caveats
docs.text:
• POST /api/tournament/reset is limited to the machine running the server, judged on the connection's peer address and on the request's Host, which must be a loopback name. X-Forwarded-For and similar headers are not consulted. The Host rule means a web page whose domain was rebound to 127.0.0.1 in a browser on the server machine is refused. Behind a reverse proxy on the same machine, every request arrives from the proxy's loopback address, so the reset is reachable by whoever the proxy exposes it to; block that path at the proxy or run with --lock-password (which 404s POST /api/tournament/reset).
  • Locked mode has no bcrypt brute-force protection. The server runs a full bcrypt comparison (bcrypt.DefaultCost approx 50-100 ms) on every X-Tournament-Password header, but does not throttle repeated failed attempts. For internet-exposed locked-mode deployments, add a reverse proxy that rate-limits authenticated routes (for example, nginx's limit_req).
  • Mode switching preserves the stored password. Switching from file mode to locked mode does NOT erase tournament.md's password field; auth stops consulting it. A later switch back to file mode resurrects the original password. This is a deliberate rollback feature, but anyone with filesystem access can still read the value. To fully retire a file-mode credential before going locked, POST /api/tournament/reset it to a one-time throwaway first.

docs.title: Competition configuration
docs.text:
A competition's pool and knockout settings are stored in its competitions/<id>/config.md YAML front matter, and are exposed by the API in JSON. Key names differ between the two:

config.md key JSON API key Values Default Description extra_qualifiers extraQualifiers "", "larger-pools", "fill-bracket" "" (standard) How many finishers each pool sends to the knockout. Only meaningful for a Mixed competition with a minimum-players-per-pool size; requires pool_winners: 1 (poolWinners: 1 in JSON) for either non-default value. Refer to How many qualify from each pool. When updating a competition through the API, leaving the JSON key out keeps whatever is already stored; send the key with an empty string to set a competition back to standard.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Local LAN, file mode, default port:

bracket-creator mobile-app -f ./tournament-data

Bind to all interfaces on a custom port:

bracket-creator mobile-app -f ./tournament-data -b 0.0.0.0 -p 8082

Locked mode for a public deployment, with the hash generated as shown under Locked mode:

HASH=$(printf '%s' "$MY_ADMIN_SECRET" | bracket-creator hash-password)
TOURNAMENT_PASSWORD_HASH="$HASH" \
  bracket-creator mobile-app --lock-password -f /var/lib/bracket-creator -b 0.0.0.0

docs.title: print
docs.text:
Renders bracket Excel workbooks into grouped, print-ready PDFs (competitor tags, name sheets, bracket trees, and more) using LibreOffice.

bracket-creator print --type <type> (--input <dir> | --tournament-data <dir>) [flags]

This is the command-line counterpart of the tournament app's Export PDFs button. Both share the same rendering engine. Use the CLI when you want PDFs without running the server, or when you want to generate them on a separate, LibreOffice-equipped machine. Refer to When to use the CLI.

docs.title: Input modes
docs.text:
Provide exactly one:

Flag What it reads --input <dir> A directory of pre-existing bracket .xlsx files (for example, output from create-pools or create-knockout). --tournament-data <dir> A tournament app data directory; the workbooks are generated on the fly from competition state.

Some competitions can be left out of the booklet

With --tournament-data, a competition is skipped, rather than aborting the whole booklet, when it has nothing renderable:

  • A Swiss competition has no pools and no fixed bracket, so there is nothing to lay out on a printed sheet yet. To follow a Swiss competition on the day, use the live standings view in the tournament app instead.
  • A competition whose stored bracket no longer matches its current settings cannot be rendered until the draw is regenerated or the settings are restored. That happens, for example, when the qualifier count was changed after the bracket was built.

Each skipped competition is named in a warning on the console. Every other competition still prints as usual. By default the command still exits successfully, even if every competition was skipped. Pass --fail-on-skip-all to make a scripted run detect that case.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
--type selects which sheets to render (required):

Type Output registration The data sheet from every workbook names The "Names to Print" sheets, A3 landscape, with title pages tags The competitor "Tags" sheets, with title pages (team workbooks excluded). Tags carry a QR code when the tournament's public URL is set. pools-trees Pool Draw + Tree sheets (a participant booklet), page-numbered full-bracket Pool Draw + Pool/Elimination Matches + Trees, page-numbered all Every type, written into --output-dir

docs.title: Other flags
docs.text:
Flag Short Default Description --output -o (none) Output PDF path for a single --type. Mutually exclusive with --output-dir. --output-dir (none) Output directory. Required for --type=all; for a single --type, give this or --output. --team-file any filename containing team An .xlsx basename to treat as a team workbook (excluded from tags). Repeatable. --fail-on-skip-all off Exit with a non-zero status if every competition was skipped, so a scripted run can detect that no booklet was produced. Refer to Some competitions can be left out of the booklet.

An output target is always required. For a single --type, provide exactly one of --output or --output-dir. --type=all requires --output-dir and rejects --output.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Generate every PDF group from a folder of bracket workbooks:

bracket-creator print --type=all --input=./xlsx/ --output-dir=./pdfs

Generate everything from a tournament-data directory:

bracket-creator print --type=all --tournament-data=tournament-data/ --output-dir=./pdfs

Competitor tags only, to a single file:

bracket-creator print --type=tags --input=./xlsx/ -o ./tags.pdf

docs.title: When to use the CLI
docs.text:
The tournament app's in-app export needs LibreOffice in the running server. The CLI lets you keep the server on the lean default image (no LibreOffice) and render PDFs elsewhere:

  • Offline / CLI-only events: you built brackets with create-pools or the Legacy Web UI and never ran the tournament app. Only the CLI can render those into PDFs (--input).
  • Out-of-band generation: run print --tournament-data ... on a LibreOffice-equipped machine instead of bundling LibreOffice into every deployment.
  • Batch or scripted PDF generation.

docs.title: LibreOffice requirement
docs.text: print renders through LibreOffice (soffice). Install it with your platform's package manager (ensuring soffice is on PATH), or set $LIBREOFFICE_PATH to the soffice binary. If LibreOffice is not found, the command exits with installation instructions. The published bracket-creator-mobile-pdf image bundles it.

docs.title: serve
docs.text:
Starts the web UI so you can generate brackets from a browser without using the command line.

bracket-creator serve [flags]

docs.title: Flags
docs.text: Flag Short Default Description --port -p 8080 (or $PORT) Port to listen on --bind -b localhost (or $BIND_ADDRESS) Address to bind to

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Start with the defaults. The UI is at http://localhost:8080:

bracket-creator serve

Use a different port:

bracket-creator serve -p 8081

Make it reachable from other machines on the network:

bracket-creator serve -b 0.0.0.0

Refer to the Legacy Web UI guide for a walkthrough of the interface.

docs.title: Take part in a self-run tournament
docs.text:
A self-run tournament lets competitors and table helpers run and score their own matches with no admin password. The organiser turns this on when creating the tournament. For the full rules of self-run and officiated modes, refer to Operating modes.

The steps on this page apply only to a self-run tournament. In an officiated tournament, an operator carries out these actions for you.

docs.title: Register yourself
docs.text:
When the tournament is self-run, a public self-registration page is open for individual competitions while they are still in setup, before the organiser generates the draw. Open the registration page on your own device and enter your details to join a competition.

The public self-registration form: name, dojo, optional dan grade.

Note

Self-registration is not available for team competitions; the organiser adds the team roster directly. In an officiated tournament, the registration page is not available at all, and the organiser adds you to the competition directly.

If the form says someone with your name is already registered, your name and dojo are already on the list and you are done. A namesake from another dojo registers normally. If you are a different person with the same name at the same dojo, ask the organiser to add you.

docs.title: Check-in
docs.text: Self-run mode has no check-in. There is nothing to mark on the day: the draw includes everyone on the roster, so make sure your name is on it before the organiser generates the draw.

docs.title: Report your own score
docs.text:
You can record your match result directly from the public viewer, without the admin password. A result you enter is tagged as self-reported; a result entered by an operator is tagged as admin.

Only everyday match outcomes are available to self-reporters. Decisions that require an official ruling remain with the operator, and so do destructive actions such as deleting a competition or discarding a draw. For a full list of outcomes and what they mean, refer to Recording decisions.

When a knockout team match finishes level, you can add the representative bout (daihyosen) from the score sheet, score it like any other bout, and finish the match on the winner it decides. A kachinuki match has no representative bout: a tied pairing that must produce a result is settled by encho on that same bout (refer to Scoring a kachinuki encounter). A representative bout added by mistake can be removed while it is still unscored, until the match finishes; after that, only the organiser can add or remove one. The score sheet does not offer a judges' decision (hantei): that stays with the organiser, on the representative bout as on every other bout. When the organiser records one, the score sheet shows the representative bout as decided and you cannot change it, but you can still finish the match on that decision.

In a team match you can also name each bout's fighters on the score sheet: pick a team member from the list, or type their name. The names are saved with the match. Once the match has finished, ask the organiser to correct a name. The score sheet can bring a team up to twice its team size plus two members; to add more, or to name anyone once the competition has finished, ask the organiser.

docs.title: If your result cannot be sent
docs.text: If your device cannot send a result you entered, because there is no connection or the server keeps refusing it, the app keeps it on the device and sends it when it can. While that is so, a count of unsent results appears in the bottom-left corner of the public page, but nothing is shown while a result is simply being sent. Tap the count to see what is held and whether each item is waiting for the connection or being refused. An item the server keeps refusing has a Discard button: after you confirm, that item alone is discarded, so you can check the match and enter the result again if it is still needed. An item that is only waiting for the connection cannot be discarded; it is sent automatically when the connection returns.

docs.title: Follow your matches and standings
docs.text:
To track your progress, view the draw, and see standings, refer to Following a tournament.

The public home in self-run mode: each open competition carries a Register button.

docs.title: Record match decisions
docs.text: Not every bout is decided on points. The score editor records the kendo outcomes described here. Open the score editor from the Scores tab on a competition page, or from a match card in the court console (refer to Score a match).

docs.title: Kiken (withdrawal)
docs.text:
Kiken covers two distinct situations with different consequences.

Pick the side that withdrew: no side is chosen for you, and Record stays unavailable until you pick one. Once you do, the button names it (for example Record: AKA withdrew) and a line beneath says who cannot fight again and who wins the match.

docs.title: Voluntary withdrawal (FIK Article 31)
docs.text: A voluntary kiken is permanent. The competitor takes no further matches in this competition and cannot be reinstated.

docs.title: Injury withdrawal (FIK Article 30)
docs.text: An injury kiken can be reinstated later by the operator if the competitor recovers and is fit to continue. Until reinstated, the competitor is blocked from starting any further match.

docs.title: Fusenpai and fusensho
docs.text:
Fusenpai is the no-show decision: the competitor who did not appear forfeits the match.

Pick the side that did not show up: no side is chosen for you, and Record stays unavailable until you pick one. Once you do, the button names it (for example Record: SHIRO did not show up).

Fusensho is used in team matches when the opposing team fields a vacant position, awarding that bout to the other side. It is also the decision the app records for the match itself when you record the win for the opponent of an already-barred competitor; refer to Matches after a competitor is barred. When neither team has a fighter for a position, record that bout as a Tie instead.

A kiken, fusenpai, or fusensho awards the winner the match points without a technique, and each awarded point is recorded as a circle. This follows the FIK Regulations of Kendo Shiai and Shinpan (Article 32 and the score board appendix). The winner's score shows two circles, or a single circle during overtime, when only the one deciding point is awarded. Any point the withdrawing side had already scored stays valid and is kept on the sheet. In a team match, the sub-bouts already fought are preserved and still count toward the standings.

To undo a per-bout fusensho, tap the pressed Fusensho button again. The circles are removed and any point already scored stays. To correct a point the other side scored, tap that mark to remove it: the fusensho stays. Fusensho cannot be given to a side whose opponent has already won the bout with two points: the button is greyed out, and tapping it shows why. Clear those points first if the bout was not really won, undoing that opponent's own fusensho first if it has one.

When a kiken, fusenpai, or fusensho decides a regular team match, every bout that has no result yet is also credited to the other team, 2-0 each: one individual victory and two points, the same figures a fusensho bout scores. This shows up wherever the match does: the individual victories and points totals, the standings, the bout rows, and the exported workbook. Bouts already fought keep their own results. Kachinuki encounters are unaffected, because they end on whichever bout the operator chooses, not on every position being filled.

docs.title: Hikiwake
docs.text: A hikiwake is a draw. It applies in pool, league, and Swiss matches, and in the individual bouts of a team encounter in any phase. A knockout match itself cannot end in a draw. A hikiwake contributes to the standings separately from wins and losses. To record one, tap Mark draw between the two sides in the score editor; in a team encounter, tap Tie (hikiwake) on the bout's row.

docs.title: Encho (overtime)
docs.text:
Encho is the extra period played when a match is level at the end of regulation and must still produce a winner. That is usually a knockout match, but an individual pool match can also go to encho when the tournament's rules call for it. A team pool encounter is not extended: a tie there is a draw, and teams still level on the pool standings play a daihyosen instead. Encho follows ippon-shobu rules: the first competitor to score wins.

An individual knockout match cannot be finished level. While the score is tied, the Finish button reads Needs a winner instead: fight encho, then record a hantei if the competitors are still level after it.

To record a hantei, tap Decide by hantei and pick the winning side. Each button names the side's colour and competitor, for example SHIRO (White) wins: Tanaka and AKA (Red) wins: Yamada. Then finish the match as usual: Finish (on the court console, Finish + Start Next) and tap it again to confirm, or Save correction when you are correcting a result. Picking a side on its own records nothing, so a slip of the thumb between the two buttons can be put right before anything is saved.

In the score editor, open the Overtime control and tick Encho started. A counter appears so you can record how many overtime periods were fought, using the + and - buttons. The counter starts at 1 and has no upper limit. How many periods are fought, and how a match still level after them is finally settled, is the shimpan's call. That may be a judges' decision for an individual bout, or a daihyosen for a team encounter. Record what actually happened on court, however many periods that took.

Completed results follow the paper score sheet's layout. The centre, between the two sides' points, only ever carries one mark: vs when no special mark applies, X for a tie, (E) for a match that went to overtime, or (DH) for a team encounter sent to a representative bout. The marks never combine: a match that went to encho cannot end in a tie, and a daihyosen has no overtime. A side with no points shows a plain dash. A match won by men in regulation reads M vs –, and the same win in overtime reads M (E) –, on the court console and the public viewer. The exported results workbook carries the same (E) marker in its centre column, but leaves a no-points cell blank rather than dashed. The marker is the same however many overtime periods were fought, because the counter records the number for the tournament log but results never show it.

Everything else is a result, written beside the competitor it names: Ht next to the winner of a judges' decision, Kiken next to the competitor who withdrew, Fus. next to a no-show, and also Fus. next to the winner when the match itself was decided by a fusensho. A match decided by hantei after a tied overtime reads M Ht (E) K, with the winner's mark on the winner's side of the centre. A team encounter shows its team totals in the score cell instead, so its marks sit where they happened. A bout's own mark (X, (E), or Ht for a representative bout decided by the judges) appears on that bout's row wherever the bouts are shown, such as the score editor, the match's page on the public viewer and the court display. A decision that settles the encounter is marked beside the team on the bracket and wherever the match is listed: Kiken beside a team that withdrew, Fus. beside a team that did not appear, and Fus. beside the winning team when the encounter was closed with a fusensho. On the bracket, the encounter also shows its winner with a tick, and (DH) when a representative bout decided it. The exported workbook carries each numbered bout's marks on its row, Kiken or Fus. beside the team's victory count, and X (a drawn encounter) or (DH) in the centre of the encounter's summary row; a knockout encounter's representative bout, with its Ht, is on the Representative Bouts sheet (refer to Daihyosen).

docs.title: Daihyosen
docs.text:
A daihyosen is a representative bout used to break a tie when points and ranking criteria cannot separate two teams.

It applies in two situations:

  • In the knockout phase, when a team encounter finishes level.
  • In team pool or league play, when two teams finish equal on every ranking criterion and the tie decides who advances or how they are seeded.

A tie that does not affect advancement is left as a shared rank with no extra bout. In league play, running the daihyosen is the operator's choice rather than an automatic step; refer to Team standings and tie-breaks for both options.

The bout is a single-point ippon-shobu with no time limit, between one representative from each tied team. Because it runs until someone scores, a daihyosen has no encho. The score editor lets you pick each team's representative from its roster. On the court console, the bout appears with a (DH) mark in the centre of the score. In pool and league standings, the team that won its daihyosen carries a DH badge.

When a knockout team encounter is settled by a representative bout, the results workbook (Export & print, then Download results (.xlsx)) lists it on a Representative Bouts sheet, one section for each such encounter. A section is titled as that encounter is on the Elimination Matches sheet, followed by (Representative bout), with White (Shiro) on the left and Red (Aka) on the right. The bout's row shows DH where a numbered bout shows its number, then each team's representative with their number and name, the score, (DH) in the centre column, and the result mark (Ht, Kiken or Fus.) beside the side it names. A side whose representative was not picked shows no name. The sheet appears only when at least one encounter had a representative bout. The tie-break daihyosen of a team pool or league is not on it.

docs.title: Chusen (drawing lots)
docs.text:
Chusen is the last resort when two or more tied teams have played a round of daihyosen and the bouts still do not produce a strict order. Examples are a cycle where each team beats another, an all-drawn round, or two teams finishing level on daihyosen wins.

When chusen is required, the Pools tab (labelled League for league competitions) shows a "Chusen (drawing lots) required" panel listing the tied teams. Draw lots offline, enter each team's finishing position in the panel, and record it to settle the order and let the competition advance.

In a competition with pools and then a knockout, the panel can also appear after the knockout has started, when a corrected pool result leaves a tie that only chusen can settle. The knockout match that the tied place feeds waits until you record the positions.

The positions you record decide who goes through. If they change who holds a qualifying place after the old holder has already fought a knockout match, the app asks first, in the same way as for a corrected pool result: it names who moves and which match was fought, and Apply and reopen records the positions and reopens that match for the new qualifier. If that knockout match is being fought right now, the positions are not recorded until it is finished or sent back to the queue. Refer to Correct a pool result after the knockout has started.

Chusen is the only place ranks are set by hand, and it happens only when the bouts themselves cannot decide the order.

docs.title: Change a chusen recorded in the wrong order
docs.text:
After you record a chusen, the same tab shows a "Chusen (drawing lots) recorded" panel with the order you recorded, for example "Drawing lots: 1st Kyoto, 2nd Osaka, 3rd Nara". If you entered the order wrongly, select Change. The entry opens again with the recorded positions filled in. Enter the order the lots actually gave and record it, or select Cancel to leave the recorded order as it is.

A changed order can change who qualifies from the pool. The app treats it the same as a first chusen, and checks the new order as a whole, so it only asks about a team whose place actually changes: if a team moves out of a knockout match that has already been fought, it asks first, and Apply and reopen reopens that match for the new qualifier. If that match is being fought right now, the change is not recorded until the match is finished or sent back to the queue.

docs.title: Competitor eligibility after a decision
docs.text: A kiken or fusenpai marks the competitor who withdrew or did not appear as ineligible for further matches. The app blocks starting an ineligible competitor, so a withdrawn competitor cannot silently re-enter the draw. An injury kiken (FIK Article 30) can be reversed: once the operator reinstates the competitor, the eligibility block is lifted and they can fight again.

docs.title: Matches after a competitor is barred
docs.text:
A barred competitor's other scheduled matches cannot be started, so the app steers everyone around them instead of leaving a dead entry in the queue. They are skipped by Up next, Finish + Start Next, the shiai-jo display's next line, the lobby view, and on-deck alerts, so nobody is nudged to warm up for a bout that cannot be fought. On the public schedule, the pools, and the bracket, the barred competitor's name carries a Withdrawn mark.

On the court console queue, the Scores tab, and the score editor, the match instead carries a note explaining why (for example "Kyoto withdrew: record the fusensho.") and a button naming the opponent, for example Record fusensho for Sato. One tap records the match as a fusensho for the opponent, without touching the barred competitor's eligibility record. For an injury kiken, a Reinstate button naming the barred competitor sits alongside it, restoring eligibility so the match can be fought instead. Once recorded, the match reads, for example, "Recorded: Fusensho for Sato. Kyoto had withdrawn.", with a Clear fusensho action if it was recorded by mistake: it reopens the match, back to the queue if the competitor is still barred (record the fusensho again, or reinstate them first; a match going back to the queue takes no court, so another match running on that court does not stop it), or back to in progress, ready to score, if they have since been reinstated.

Recording a kiken or fusenpai changes only that match. It does not do anything to the withdrawn competitor's other scheduled matches: each one shows its own notice and one-tap Record fusensho for <opponent> button, described above, when it comes up in the queue or you open it in the score editor. As with Finish + Start Next, the court console then starts the court's next match in the same competition, passing over the withdrawn competitor's own. The Scores tab never starts a match by itself, so start the next one from its row. The app never switches you to another competition or court by itself.

You can also open one of the competitor's other matches in the score editor and record Fusenpai for the barred competitor. The match records a fusenpai against them, and their eligibility record still names the match where they withdrew, so an injury kiken can still be reinstated. That match then offers Clear fusenpai, which works as it does for a fusensho: while the competitor is still withdrawn, the match goes back to the queue.
